title: Hypothermia
why_this_matters: Hypothermia can follow environmental exposure, illness, medications, anesthesia or trauma, and even severely affected dogs, including those in cardiopulmonary arrest, can recover completely with appropriate therapy [1].

what_changes_from_human.point: Ordinary thermometers can miss hypothermia: nontraditional thermometers may be needed to diagnose it [1].
Even dogs in cardiopulmonary arrest from hypothermia can recover fully, so resuscitation may need to be prolonged [1].

recognition: Hypothermia is diagnosed from presenting temperature or clinical signs, and may need nontraditional thermometers [1].
Human trauma data: hypothermia on admission was independently associated with higher mortality (23.4% vs 2.3%) in a 3-million-patient registry. This is human data and is context only [2].
management: Rewarming is the primary treatment for accidental hypothermia, from passive surface rewarming to extracorporeal rewarming. The goal is to return core temperature to a level that restores normal physiologic function [1].
Intravenous fluids and other supportive care are typically indicated. If cardiopulmonary arrest is present, prolonged resuscitation may be required [1].
In secondary hypothermia, reversing the underlying cause is important [1].
There are few prognostic indicators in hypothermic dogs, so early discouraging findings should not stop care [1].

takeaway: Stop the heat loss, rewarm, and keep resuscitating: a cold dog can still recover.
